lead.headline: Build a robot, solve an adventure: programming becomes play
body: Adventure games are putting a new question to the home computer: can the player build the intelligence that wins the game? In the April–May Computer Gaming World, Gregg Williams compares Robot Odyssey I and Chipwits, two simulations that make programming itself the entertainment. These are current review selections, not announcements of releases during this week.

Robot Odyssey I, from The Learning Co., lists at $49.95 for the Apple II. Its Innovation Lab gives players room to experiment before tackling Robotropolis. Sensors feed digital-logic gates; wires turn those signals into robot behavior. Players can watch signals propagate and work through three tutorial worlds before the five adventure levels described in the review.

Chipwits takes a different route on the Macintosh. Its domino-shaped visual instructions assemble into programs in a Workshop, then face eight missions. The review’s publisher box identifies Brainpower and a $59.95 price. Williams finds both games engaging but considers Chipwits the gentler introduction for a programming newcomer.

The attraction is not simply watching a robot obey. A failed mission sends the player back to the design bench to discover what the instructions actually mean. The review reports an Apple II Chipwits edition expected by publication and a Commodore 64 version licensed to Epyx; these remain reported plans rather than verified shipping dates.
lead.dek: Robot Odyssey I and Chipwits make circuits and visual instructions the machinery of adventure.

stories.headline: AT competition widens: three rivals promise more choice
body: The April 29 Computerworld surveys three more entrants in the AT-compatible contest: Corona, Zenith and Televideo. Their announcements came the previous week, but the new comparison gives buyers a timely look at the widening Intel 80286 field.

Zenith’s Z-200 standard package is listed at $3,999 with 512 KB, a 1.2 MB floppy, six AT-compatible slots and MS-DOS 3.1. Its enhanced version is $5,599. Zenith promotes no-wait-state memory; that is a vendor claim, not an independent benchmark.

Televideo quotes $3,400 for a standard 256 KB machine and $4,995 for an enhanced 512 KB system with a 20 MB hard disk. It offers 8 MHz operation with a switch to 6 MHz. Corona’s 38-pound transportable includes a nine-inch green screen; its $4,500 standard configuration has 512 KB and two floppy drives. Both companies promise July shipments, not immediate shelf availability.

stories.headline: Buyers and vendors still divided over software protection
body: Software buyers and vendors remain divided over protection. Kathleen Burton reports in the April 29 Computerworld that the Microcomputer Managers Association and Adapso have not resolved their differences over proposed standards.

The MMA says its members bought more than $100 million in microcomputer software last year. Hardware keys and the administrative burden of tracking software keys are among the practical concerns. MMA president Alan Gross denies any softening of his association’s position.

Adapso counsel Ron Palenski cites antitrust considerations in explaining why the association cannot recommend marketing methods. Lotus president Mitchell Kapor acknowledges that user groups represent enough of the community to require engagement, yet the report describes no vendor plan to refocus the protection strategy. This is an ownership and usability dispute, not evidence of a named pirate crew.

stories.headline: Share a screen over the telephone
body: The telephone line is becoming a shared workbench. New-product coverage in the April 29 Computerworld describes CC:share, which lets separated users run applications together, see screen activity and pass control of the keyboard.

Professional and Corporate Communication Systems suggests training, presentations and remote maintenance. File transfer and screen snapshots stored as PC-DOS files extend the session beyond conversation. The related CC:mail can capture application screens, attach files, and supply word-processing, drawing and highlighting functions.

Both products target IBM PC, XT, AT and compatible machines with DOS 2.0 or later and a Hayes-compatible modem. CC:share needs 26 KB beyond the application’s requirements; CC:mail needs 320 KB RAM. Quoted prices are $195 and $295 per copy respectively in purchases of ten, not single-copy retail offers.

worldAnchor.headline: Reagan visits Bitburg and Bergen-Belsen
worldAnchor.summary: On May 5, President Reagan visits Bergen-Belsen and takes part in the controversial Bitburg cemetery visit. His Bitburg Air Base remarks acknowledge the controversy while arguing for German-American reconciliation.

curiosity.headline: Commodore offers worn-out game disks a $5 second life
curiosity.summary: A small service-policy change earns praise in the April–May gaming press.
curiosity.detail: Computer Gaming World’s Commodore column reports a $5 replacement policy for Commodore diskettes damaged or worn through continued use, with return within ten days. This is the policy as reported in the period column, not a modern guarantee or a new-this-week announcement.
